title: Foundations of Evolutionary Psychology
description: Darwin, adaptation, and the long road from biology to behaviour

concepts.title: Natural and Sexual Selection
concepts.contentHtml:
Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) introduced natural selection: heritable traits that increase survival and reproduction become more common across generations. The mechanism is mechanical and unintelligent — variation, inheritance, and differential reproductive success.

In The Descent of Man (1871) Darwin added sexual selection, the differential reproductive success caused by competition for mates. Sexual selection explains traits costly to survival — the peacock's tail, the stag's antlers, the elaborate songs of birds — because they boost mating success more than they reduce viability.

Sexual selection comes in two forms: intrasexual (members of one sex compete with each other, often males fighting for access to females) and intersexual (the choosier sex, typically females, prefers certain traits in mates). Both leave evolutionary fingerprints on body, brain, and behaviour.

Evolutionary psychology applies these principles to the human mind: psychological mechanisms, like physical organs, are products of selection.

concepts.title: Inclusive Fitness and Hamilton's Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical Darwinism struggled to explain altruism — behaviour that costs the actor while benefiting another. Why would worker bees forgo reproduction to raise a queen's offspring?

W.D. Hamilton's 1964 papers solved the puzzle with inclusive fitness: a gene can spread either by helping its carrier reproduce or by helping relatives, who share copies of it. Fitness is reckoned across all carriers of the gene, not just the individual body.

Hamilton's rule formalises the condition for an altruistic gene to spread: rB > C, where r is genetic relatedness, B is the benefit to the recipient, and C the cost to the actor. Siblings share r = 0.5, cousins 0.125. Hence J.B.S. Haldane's quip that he would lay down his life for two brothers or eight cousins.

This single insight unified eusociality in insects, parental care, and helping behaviour across taxa, and reframed the gene — not the individual — as the unit of selection.

concepts.title: Trivers: Parental Investment and Reciprocal Altruism
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Trivers extended the framework with two influential papers. The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism (1971) showed that altruism between non-kin can evolve when actors interact repeatedly and can detect cheaters: 'I'll scratch your back if you'll scratch mine.' This explains cooperation in vampire bats, primates, and humans.

Parental Investment and Sexual Selection (1972) generalised Bateman's principle: the sex that invests more in offspring (typically females, who bear gestation and lactation costs) becomes the limiting reproductive resource. The lower-investing sex competes for access; the higher-investing sex chooses.

This framework predicts robust patterns: in species with high female investment, males compete and females choose; in species with reversed roles (sea horses, jacanas), the pattern reverses. Trivers' analysis provides the engine behind much of evolutionary psychology's account of human sex differences in mating.

The framework is descriptive, not prescriptive — explaining behavioural tendencies, not justifying them.

title: The Adapted Mind
description: Modularity, the EEA, and the cheater-detection module

concepts.title: The Environment of Evolutionary Adaptedness
concepts.contentHtml:
John Bowlby coined the term environment of evolutionary adaptedness (EEA), and Leda Cosmides and John Tooby placed it at the centre of evolutionary psychology in The Adapted Mind (1992).

The EEA is not a single place or time but the statistical composite of selection pressures that shaped a given adaptation. For most human psychological traits, the relevant EEA is the Pleistocene — roughly two million years of small-group, hunter-gatherer life on the African savannah and beyond.

The point is that selection takes many generations to track environmental change. Modern environments — refined sugar, contraception, online dating, mass anonymity — differ radically from ancestral ones. Many puzzling modern behaviours and pathologies (obesity, anxiety in dense cities, attraction to processed foods) make sense as mismatches between Pleistocene-tuned mechanisms and novel environments.

The EEA is a methodological lens, not a Garden of Eden: ancestral life was demanding, and the concept is best treated as a research heuristic rather than a precise reconstruction.

concepts.title: Massive Modularity
concepts.contentHtml:
Cosmides and Tooby argued that the mind is not a general-purpose computer but a collection of domain-specific modules — specialised mechanisms shaped by selection to solve recurrent ancestral problems: face recognition, kin detection, mate choice, foraging, predator avoidance, language acquisition.

Their massive modularity thesis claims the architecture is modular through and through. Steven Pinker's How the Mind Works (1997) popularised the analogy: the mind is a Swiss army knife of evolved tools, not a blank slate.

Critics like Jerry Fodor (who originally introduced modularity in a narrower sense) argue that central cognition — belief fixation, analogy, planning — is too flexible to be modular. Others worry that 'module' is defined so loosely it becomes unfalsifiable.

A more defensible version: the mind contains many evolved biases and learning specialisations, even if they aren't strictly encapsulated modules in Fodor's technical sense.

concepts.title: The Wason Selection Task and Cheater Detection
concepts.contentHtml:
Cosmides' best-known empirical case concerns reasoning. Peter Wason's selection task asks participants to test a conditional rule by turning over cards. With abstract content (e.g., 'If a card has a vowel, then it has an even number'), most people fail — only around 10–25% reason correctly.

But change the content to a social contract ('If you drink alcohol, you must be over 21') and performance leaps to 65–80%. People readily detect potential cheaters even when the underlying logic is identical.

Cosmides argued this asymmetry reveals an evolved cheater-detection module: humans evolved as obligate cooperators, so detecting people who take benefits without paying costs would have been fitness-critical.

The result is replicable, but interpretation is contested. Critics suggest familiarity, deontic framing, or general pragmatic reasoning could account for the effect without a dedicated module. The case illustrates how evolutionary hypotheses generate testable predictions — and the difficulty of cleanly distinguishing rival explanations.

title: Mating, Kin, and Cooperation
description: Mate choice, the grandmother hypothesis, and the evolution of helping

concepts.title: Buss and the Cross-Cultural Study of Mate Preferences
concepts.contentHtml:
David Buss' 1989 study surveyed 10,047 participants across 37 cultures on six continents. Predictions derived from parental investment theory: women, the higher-investing sex, should weight cues to resource provisioning more heavily; men should weight cues to fertility — particularly youth and physical health.

Results showed broad cross-cultural regularities: in all 37 cultures, men rated youth and physical attractiveness more highly than women did; in 36 of 37, women rated good financial prospects more highly than men did. Both sexes universally valued kindness, intelligence, and emotional stability.

The pattern is one of the most-replicated findings in cross-cultural psychology, but interpretation is contested. Social role theorists (Alice Eagly, Wendy Wood) argue the differences track patriarchal economic structures: where women have economic power, the gap narrows. Defenders reply that the pattern persists even in egalitarian Scandinavia.

The honest summary: stable sex differences in stated preferences exist; their precise causes blend evolved psychology and cultural ecology.

concepts.title: Kin Selection in Humans and the Grandmother Hypothesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Hamilton's rule predicts that humans should preferentially help close relatives, and they do: studies of life-or-death help, inheritance, childcare, and emotional closeness all show steep relatedness gradients. People also discriminate between maternal and paternal kin in ways that track paternity uncertainty — maternal grandmothers tend to invest more, on average, than paternal grandfathers.

Humans are unusual in another respect: women undergo menopause, a long post-reproductive lifespan, which is rare in mammals. The grandmother hypothesis (Kristen Hawkes and colleagues, drawing on Hadza foragers) proposes that older women boosted their inclusive fitness more by provisioning grandchildren than by continuing to bear children themselves.

Evidence is mixed but suggestive: grandmaternal presence is associated with lower child mortality in pre-modern populations across continents. Alternative explanations include the embodied capital hypothesis and life-history trade-offs.

Either way, the puzzle of menopause shows how evolutionary thinking generates falsifiable hypotheses about human life history.

concepts.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Axelrod's The Evolution of Cooperation (1984) ran computer tournaments of the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. The simple strategy tit-for-tat — cooperate first, then copy your partner's last move — won repeatedly. It is nice, retaliatory, forgiving, and clear.

Beyond direct reciprocity, humans cooperate via indirect reciprocity: helping those with good reputations, even toward strangers (Nowak and Sigmund). This helps explain the importance of gossip, public displays of generosity, and shame.

The contested frontier is group selection. Elliott Sober and David Sloan Wilson argue that selection sometimes operates between groups, favouring traits that benefit the group at individual cost. Steven Pinker, Richard Dawkins, and most evolutionary psychologists argue the same data are better captured by inclusive fitness, multilevel selection re-described.

The debate is partly empirical, partly definitional. What is uncontroversial: human ultra-cooperation is real, distinctively extensive, and almost certainly the product of multiple intersecting mechanisms.

title: Emotions, Disgust, and Language
description: Evolved feelings, the parasite-avoidance system, and the language instinct

concepts.title: Emotions as Adaptations
concepts.contentHtml:
Following Darwin's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872), evolutionary psychologists treat emotions as specialised programs that coordinate cognition, physiology, and behaviour to solve recurrent adaptive problems.

Fear coordinates threat-avoidance; anger renegotiates bargaining position after exploitation; jealousy guards reproductive interests; gratitude tracks willingness to reciprocate; guilt motivates repair after damaging valuable relationships.

Paul Ekman's cross-cultural studies argued for a small set of basic emotions with universal facial expressions — recognised even by isolated populations. Critics like Lisa Feldman Barrett argue emotions are constructed concepts that vary across cultures.

A reasonable synthesis: there are evolved affect programs, but their conceptual labels and surface expressions are partly shaped by culture and language. The evolutionary view does not require pure universality, only that emotions are functional rather than arbitrary.

concepts.title: Disgust and the Behavioural Immune System
concepts.contentHtml:
Valerie Curtis and others propose that disgust evolved as part of a behavioural immune system — a first line of defence against pathogens and parasites, complementary to the cellular immune system.

Cross-cultural surveys show robust disgust elicitors: bodily fluids, decay, festering wounds, certain insects, and unfamiliar foods that signal pathogen risk. Pregnant women, immunologically vulnerable, show heightened disgust sensitivity in the first trimester.

Disgust generalises beyond pathogens. Sexual disgust tracks fitness-reducing partnerships (incest, signs of disease). Moral disgust tracks norm violations: cheating, hypocrisy, betrayal. Whether moral disgust is a true extension of pathogen disgust or a metaphor that recruits its expressive vocabulary remains debated.

The behavioural immune system has been linked to xenophobia and conformity under disease threat — sobering evidence that adaptive ancient mechanisms can produce harmful modern outcomes when their inputs are mis-triggered.

concepts.title: Language as an Instinct
concepts.contentHtml:
Steven Pinker's The Language Instinct (1994) argued that human language is a biological adaptation — a complex, species-typical, universally acquired system shaped by natural selection for communication.

Evidence cited: every human society has language; deaf children spontaneously create sign systems (Nicaraguan Sign Language); pidgins become structured creoles within a generation; specific developmental disorders (specific language impairment) affect language while sparing general intelligence.

The discovery of FOXP2, a gene whose disruption causes severe speech and language deficits in the KE family, is sometimes called the 'language gene' — though more accurately a transcription factor influencing many neural systems involved in fine motor control.

Noam Chomsky himself is sceptical that language is an adaptation in the strong adaptationist sense, arguing it may have arisen as a side-effect of brain reorganisation. The debate illustrates a recurring evolutionary-psychology question: when does a complex trait demand selectionist explanation, and when can drift, byproduct, or saltation suffice?

title: Critiques and Limits
description: Spandrels, just-so stories, replication, and gene-culture coevolution

concepts.title: Spandrels of San Marco
concepts.contentHtml:
In their celebrated 1979 paper The Spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian Paradigm, Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin attacked what they called the adaptationist programme — the assumption that every trait must be an optimised adaptation.

Their image: the spandrels of the basilica of San Marco are the curved triangular spaces between arches, decoratively painted but architecturally a byproduct of placing a dome on rounded arches. They are not for anything; they are a structural side-effect.

Gould and Lewontin argued many human traits could be similar byproducts (or exaptations — traits co-opted for new functions). Music, religion, mathematics, romantic love — all might be byproducts of more general cognitive systems rather than dedicated adaptations.

The critique forces evolutionary psychology to ask: what evidence distinguishes an adaptation from a byproduct? Strong answers require species-typical structure, complexity beyond chance, fitness-relevant function, and developmental reliability — not mere plausibility.

concepts.title: Just-So Stories and Falsifiability
concepts.contentHtml:
Borrowing from Rudyard Kipling, Gould accused some evolutionary psychology of telling just-so stories: post-hoc adaptive narratives that fit any finding without genuine predictive power.

The danger is real. If a finding emerges, one can confabulate an ancestral scenario that 'explains' it; if the opposite finding emerges, one can confabulate a different scenario. Without independent constraints — fossils, comparative data, genetic signatures, cross-cultural patterns, mathematical models — evolutionary explanations risk unfalsifiability.

Defenders argue good evolutionary psychology generates a priori predictions that could fail: Buss' sex-difference predictions, Cosmides' content effects, Hamilton's relatedness gradients. When predictions are made before data are collected and survive replication, the just-so accusation loses force.

The wider replication crisis in social psychology has hit some evolutionary findings — including ovulatory shift effects on mate preference — particularly hard. Intellectual honesty requires distinguishing well-evidenced claims from speculative ones.

concepts.title: Gene-Culture Coevolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Boyd and Peter Richerson's Culture and the Evolutionary Process (1985) and later Not by Genes Alone (2005) developed dual-inheritance theory: humans evolve through two interacting inheritance streams, genetic and cultural.

Culture is not a thin overlay on biology. Cultural learning — selectively copying successful or prestigious models — is itself an evolved capacity, and it transforms the selection pressures genes face. The classic example is lactase persistence: dairying cultures created strong selection for adult lactose tolerance, which has spread independently in several populations within roughly 10,000 years.

Joseph Henrich's The Secret of Our Success (2015) extends this argument: humans dominate the planet not because of superior individual intelligence but because of cumulative cultural evolution, ratcheted by high-fidelity teaching and prosocial norms.

The mature view of human nature is therefore neither pure nature nor pure nurture: evolved minds and accumulated cultures co-construct one another, on different timescales but by the same logic of variation, inheritance, and selection.
